IOStreams.path("/var/exports/daily.csv").to_s == "/var/exports/daily.csv"
# => true
~~~

`#move_to` also detects other spellings of the same location, see [Operations on the store](#operations-on-the-store).

### Coming from Pathname

IOStreams paths are modeled on Ruby's `Pathname`, and most methods with the same name do the same thing. These are the
differences, each of which keeps a path working the same way wherever the file is stored:

| Pathname | IOStreams | Why |
|----------|-----------|-----|
| `Pathname("/a").join("/b")` is `/b` | `IOStreams.path("/a").join("/b")` is `/a/b`, and so is `IOStreams.path("/a") / "/b"` | An absolute name, such as one from configuration, is joined to the path, such as a root, rather than replacing it. A name can still leave the path with `..`, so restrict untrusted names with [allowed paths](#restricting-access-with-allowed-paths) |
| `join("..")` returns the parent | `join("..")` keeps `..`; use `cleanpath` or `directory` | Joining never accesses or resolves anything |
| `Pathname("a/b").join("a/b/c")` is `a/b/a/b/c` | `IOStreams.path("a/b").join("a/b/c")` is `a/b/c` | An element that is already within the path is used as it is, so a name that includes its root is not doubled |
| `mkpath` creates the whole path | `mkpath` creates the directories of a file, and `mkdir` creates the whole path | A path usually names a file, and writing a local file creates its directories anyway |
| `children` and `each_child` list every entry | `children("*.csv")` and `each_child` take a pattern like `glob`, skip directories and hidden files, and ignore case by default | The same pattern lists local, S3 and SFTP paths |
| `children` raises for a missing directory | Returns nothing for a missing path, or a file | S3 has no directories that could be missing |
| `delete` raises for a missing file | Does nothing, and returns the path | The same on every store, where checking first would be a separate request |
| `basename`, `dirname` and `relative_path_from` return a `Pathname` | They return a String; `directory` returns the directory as a path | A name on its own has no store; `basename` uses `file_name` when it is set |
| `read(length, offset)` | `read(length)` reads bytes from the start, after any decompression or decryption | A compressed or encrypted stream cannot seek |
| `each_line` without a block returns an Enumerator | `each` requires a block | The file, any temp file and any gpg process are closed when the block returns |
| Paths sort with `/` first | Paths sort by their full name, spelled as `==` compares it, see [Comparing paths](#comparing-paths) | Names include the scheme, bucket or host |
| `to_path`, so `File.exist?(pathname)` works | No `to_path`; use the methods of the path, such as `exist?` and `reader` | `File` and `Dir` only work with local files, so code that passes a path to them breaks when the configured path moves to S3 or SFTP |

## Using root paths

A root path names a location once, at startup, such as the directory or bucket that an application writes its exports
to, so that the code joins names to it with `IOStreams.join`, and never names the store itself. So the same code can
write local files in development and S3 in production, with only the configuration differing. Several roots can be
added, for example one for input files, another for output files, and another for reports, which can all point to one
location in development, and to separate buckets in production.

In an initializer:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.add_root(:default, "tmp/export")
IOStreams.add_root(:ftp, "tmp/ftp")
~~~

`:default` is used whenever `IOStreams.join` is not supplied a root:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.join("sample", "example.csv").to_s
# => "tmp/export/sample/example.csv"

IOStreams.join("sample", "example.csv", root: :ftp).to_s
# => "tmp/ftp/sample/example.csv"

IOStreams.join("sample", "example.csv").writer(:line) do |io|
  io << "Welcome"
  io << "To IOStreams"
end
~~~

To write to S3 and an SFTP server in production instead, only the initializer changes:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.add_root(:default, "s3://my-app-bucket/export")
IOStreams.add_root(:ftp, "sftp://sftp.example.org/~/ftp", username: "jack", ssh_options: {IdentityKey: ENV.fetch("SFTP_IDENTITY_KEY")})
~~~

* `IOStreams.add_root(name, *elements, **arguments)` takes a name of letters, digits and `_`, and the elements and
  arguments of `IOStreams.path`, or a path. It returns the root path.
* `IOStreams.root(name = :default)` returns a copy of the root path, and `IOStreams.roots` a copy of each one, by name.
  A name that has not been added raises `ArgumentError`, such as `Root: :exports has not been registered.`
* `IOStreams.join(*elements, root: :default)` joins the elements to a copy of the root path, see
  [Joining paths](#joining-paths).

A root is shared by the whole process, so `IOStreams.add_root` freezes it, and changing it, such as with `#option`,
raises `FrozenError`, while the copies that `IOStreams.root`, `IOStreams.roots` and `IOStreams.join` return can be
changed. The S3 request options and SFTP ssh options of a root are frozen with it, and `#mkpath` and `#mkdir` on a
frozen SFTP path return a copy that creates the directories. A path joined to a root keeps the arguments of the root,
such as its credentials, but not the streams and options set on the root with `#stream` or `#option`, which describe
the file that the root names, so set those on each path:

~~~ruby
root = IOStreams.add_root(:exports, "/var/exports")
root.option(:gz, level: 9)
# FrozenError: can't modify frozen IOStreams::Paths::File: #<IOStreams::Paths::File:/var/exports pipeline={}>

IOStreams.join("daily.csv.gz", root: :exports).option(:gz, level: 9).write(report)
~~~

See [Configuration](config#add_root) for more examples.

## Allowed paths {#restricting-access-with-allowed-paths}

Roots and `#join` make paths easy to build, but they do not keep a name within the root: `..` leaves it, such as
`IOStreams.join("../../etc/passwd")`. When a name comes from untrusted input, such as from a user or the configuration
of a job, add allowed paths in an initializer, so that reading, writing, listing, deleting or otherwise accessing any
other path raises `IOStreams::Errors::AccessDenied`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.add_allowed_path("/var/my_app/uploads")
IOStreams.add_allowed_path("s3://my-app-bucket/export")

IOStreams.path("/var/my_app/uploads/../secrets.yml").read
# raises IOStreams::Errors::AccessDenied

IOStreams.path("/etc/passwd").allowed?
# => false
~~~

See [Allowed paths](security#allowed-paths) for how the paths of each store are compared with them.

---

# Reading and Writing

Once you have a [path](path), read it and write it with a small set of methods, a block, a line, a row or a record at
a time, so that memory use stays low however large the file is. Each method takes a mode, which says what your code
reads or writes:

| Mode | Reads or writes | Read with | Write with |
|------|-----------------|-----------|------------|
| `:stream`, the default for `#reader` and `#writer` | Bytes, a block at a time | `reader { \|io\| io.read(1024) }` | `writer { \|io\| io << data }` |
| `:line`, the default for `#each` | Lines of text | `each(:line) { \|line\| }` | `writer(:line) { \|io\| io << line }` |
| `:array` | Rows: an Array of the values of each line | `each(:array) { \|row\| }` | `writer(:array) { \|io\| io << row }` |
| `:hash` | Records: a Hash of the values of each line, by column | `each(:hash) { \|record\| }` | `writer(:hash) { \|io\| io << record }` |

The tabular format of the file, such as CSV or JSON, says how rows and records are read from lines and written as
lines, see [Tabular formats](formats).

## Reading

`#each` yields each line, row or record:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").each do |line|
  puts line
end

IOStreams.path("example.csv").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

`#each` requires a block, so that the file is closed once it has been read, rather than returning an Enumerator,
which could leave the file open if it was not read to its end. To collect the records, add each one to an Array within
the block.

`#reader` yields the stream itself, for the code that reads it: in the `:stream` mode, an IO that responds to
`#read(length = nil, outbuf = nil)`, `#readpartial` and `#eof?`. This reads 128 bytes at a time:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").reader do |io|
  while (data = io.read(128))
    p data
  end
end
~~~

`#reader` and `#writer` return the result of the block. Within the block, an S3 object or an HTTP response is read as
the block reads it, so the IO is not a `File`. Like the IO of every stream, such as of a `.gz` file, it has the methods
of an IO that read, such as `#read`, `#gets` and `#each_line`, so a library that reads an IO, such as `CSV.new(io)`,
reads it, but not `#rewind`, `#pos`, `#size` or `#path`. Where the code needs a `File`, copy the file to a local file
first, see [Copying and moving](copy_files).

`#read` returns the whole file, which is only suitable for a small one, since all of it is held in memory:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

## Writing

`#writer` yields the stream to write to:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").writer do |io|
  io << "This is "
  io << "one line\n"
end
~~~

In the `:line` mode, each value written is followed by a newline:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").writer(:line) do |io|
  io << "these"
  io << "are separate"
  io << "lines"
end
~~~

`#write` writes a whole String:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").write("Hello World\n")
~~~

The streams that the file name implies are applied as the data is written, so writing `example.csv.gz` compresses it,
and writing a path on S3 uploads it, see [Paths](path). The block decides what is kept:

* When the block returns, or leaves early, such as with `break` or `return`, everything written is kept, and the file is
  complete, whichever streams and store it uses.
* When the block raises, or its thread is killed, nothing is kept: a local file is removed, an S3 upload is aborted,
  and a file is not uploaded to SFTP or HTTP. An IO supplied to `IOStreams.stream` keeps what was written to it, but a
  compressed or encrypted stream does not end its data, so that it cannot be mistaken for a complete file.
* A write that cannot succeed raises before the file is opened, so that an existing file is kept: an option that a
  stream cannot write with, such as a compression level that is out of range, an encoding that Ruby does not know, or
  a gem that a stream needs and that is not installed.

## Lines

Lines are split at the line ending of the file, which is the first `\r\n`, `\n` or `\r` that it holds, and the line
ending is removed from each line. When it is `\r\n`, as in a file written on Windows, a `\n` alone also ends a line,
so a file whose lines end in both ways, such as a Windows file to which a program on Linux added lines, is read line by
line.

`delimiter:` splits the file at the String supplied instead, such as `delimiter: "|"`, and then only at it, so
`delimiter: "\r\n"` keeps a `\n` alone within its line. When writing, it is written after each line, `"\n"` by
default.

A quoted value of a CSV file can contain a line break, which must not end the line. Lines are split where the format
of the file expects, so `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)` keep a quoted line break within its row. So does `each(:line)`,
for a format that quotes its values, such as CSV, whether it is set with `#format` or comes from a `.csv` file name.
Supply `embedded_within:` to the `:line` mode to choose: `nil` for the physical lines of the file, or the quote
character, such as `'"'`, for the lines of a file whose format is not set:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").each(:line, embedded_within: nil) do |line|
  puts line
end
~~~

Other notes:

* A blank line is yielded as an empty String by `each(:line)`, and as `nil` by `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)`.
* Lines are read 64KB at a time, which `buffer_size:` changes, such as `each(:hash, buffer_size: 1_048_576)`.
* A line without a delimiter within 100 blocks, 6.4MB by default, raises `IOStreams::Errors::DelimiterNotFound`, rather
  than reading the whole of a file that has no line endings into memory.

## Text and binary data

Lines, rows and records are read as UTF-8 text, whichever streams the file is read through, such as gzip or PGP,
apart from [fixed width files](formats#fixed-width-files), which are read as ASCII. Data that is not valid UTF-8 raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, an `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`, whose message gives the invalid bytes,
their byte offset, and the line that they are on, once the lines before them have been read:

~~~
IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding: "\xE9" is not valid UTF-8 at byte offset 1043 on line 12
~~~

The byte order mark (U+FEFF) that programs such as Excel write at the start of a UTF-8 file is removed, so that the
first column name of a CSV file is read as it appears.

`#read` returns the whole file as UTF-8 without checking it, like `File.read`, so that it can also read a binary
file, such as an image, whose bytes are unchanged. The `:stream` mode of `#reader` reads bytes, so `io.read(128)`
returns up to 128 bytes of binary data, whether the file is plain, compressed or encrypted.

Writing writes the bytes of each String as they are, unless an encoding is set. Fixed width files are the exception:
they are written as ASCII.

### Character encoding

To read or write text in another encoding, set it on the path with `#encoding`, which describes the file, whichever
streams it has. Name the encoding of the file, and the encoding that your code reads, in Ruby's `"external:internal"`
form, as `File.read` does:

~~~ruby
# Read a Windows-1252 file as UTF-8 strings.
IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end

# Write UTF-8 strings as a Windows-1252 file, with the same setting.
IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "José"}
end
~~~

With just one encoding, such as `encoding("Windows-1252")`, the strings read are in that encoding, rather than
converted to UTF-8, and cannot be combined with UTF-8 text. `encoding("BINARY")` reads lines, rows and records as
binary strings, as IOStreams did before v3.0.

`#encoding` also takes the other options of the encode stream, which converts the text:

* `replace:` replaces each character that is not valid, or that the target encoding does not have, rather than raising,
  such as `encoding("UTF-8", replace: "?")`. With `replace: ""` such characters are removed.
* `cleaner:` cleans the text as it is read or written: `:printable` removes the characters that are not printable,
  apart from line endings, `:replace_non_printable` replaces them with `replace:`, and a Proc is called with the text
  and the `replace:` value, and returns the cleaned text.

~~~ruby
# Remove the characters that are not printable, and replace those that are not valid UTF-8 with a space.
IOStreams.path("upload.csv").encoding("UTF-8", cleaner: :printable, replace: " ").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

Each call to `#encoding` merges its options with those already set, and `#encoding` without arguments returns the
encoding that was set. An encoding that Ruby does not know, or a cleaner that is neither a built-in rule nor a Proc,
raises `ArgumentError` when it is set.

The encoding of the text is converted closest to your code, after the file is decompressed or decrypted, so
`IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").encoding("BINARY")` still decompresses the file, and reads its text as bytes.

With an encoding, the stream that `#reader` supplies reads like an IO that converts text, such as
`File.open(name, "r:Windows-1252:UTF-8")`, so a library that reads an IO, such as `CSV`, reads the text in the encoding
that your code reads:

~~~ruby
require "csv"

IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").reader do |io|
  CSV.new(io, headers: true).map(&:to_h)
end
# => [{"name" => "José", "city" => "Málaga"}]
~~~

Its `read(length)` and `#readpartial` read text too, rather than bytes: whole characters, up to `length` bytes of them,
or the first character when it is longer.

### Data as it is stored

`#raw` reads and writes the data as it is stored, without the streams that the file name implies, and without any
encoding, so that text is read and written as bytes. For example, to checksum a compressed file as it is stored, or to
write data that is already compressed:

~~~ruby
require "digest"

Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").raw.read)

IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").raw.write(gzipped_data)
~~~

`#raw` changes the path that it is called on, so that reading it afterwards also reads the stored bytes. To keep the
path as it is, call it on a copy, such as `IOStreams.path(path).raw.read`. Setting a stream, option or encoding after
`#raw` raises `ArgumentError`, and `#raw?` returns whether it was called.

To copy a file as it is stored, such as to download a zip file without unzipping it, use
`copy_to(target, convert: false)`, since `#raw` on the source would still apply the streams of the target, see
[Copying and moving](copy_files).

## Settings on the path, options for each call

A setting that describes the file is set on the path, and an option that says what your code wants from the file is
supplied to each call. A path is configuration: it can be held in a configuration system and handed to code that only
calls `each(:hash)`, so the settings of the path are all that it takes to read or write the file the right way, by
any code, including `#copy_from` and `#copy_to`.

| Setting | Where | Because it says |
|---------|-------|-----------------|
| The path or url, and `#file_name` | The path | Where the file is, and the extensions that name its streams and format |
| `#stream` and `#option` | The path | How the file is compressed or encrypted |
| `#encoding` | The path | The encoding of the text of the file |
| `#format` | The path | The tabular format of the file, such as `:json` |
| `#schema` | The path | The fields of the file and their types, which columns it can have and must have, the position of each fixed width field, and whether it has a header row |
| The mode, such as `:hash` | Each call | Whether the code reads or writes blocks, lines, rows or records |
| `delimiter:` and `buffer_size:` | Each call | How lines are split or ended, and how much is read at a time |
| `embedded_within:` | Each call, in the `:line` mode | Whether the code reads the physical lines, or the logical lines of a quoted format |

IOStreams checks where each setting is supplied:

* A setting of the path supplied to a call, such as `each(:hash, format: :json)`, raises `ArgumentError`, as do
  `file_name:`, `schema:`, `format_options:` and `default_format:`.
* An option that only applies when reading, such as `buffer_size:`, raises `ArgumentError` when it is supplied to
  `#writer`, rather than being ignored.
* Any other option that the mode does not take, such as a misspelled `delimitr:`, raises `ArgumentError` before the
  file is opened, naming the mode and listing the options that it takes.
* `#copy_from` and `#copy_to` use their options to write the target, so an option that only applies when reading
  raises `ArgumentError` for them too. The copy reads the source with the settings of the source path, so set what
  describes the source, such as its schema, on its path.

~~~ruby
# The configuration describes the file.
people = IOStreams.path(ENV["PEOPLE_PATH"]).format(:csv).schema(ENV["PEOPLE_SCHEMA"])

# The code says what it wants from it: records, whose columns the schema checks.
people.each(:hash) { |person| p person }

# A copy reads the source with the settings of its path, and writes the target with the settings of its own.
IOStreams.path("people.json").schema(fieldsMatch: "subset", fields: [{name: "name"}, {name: "age"}]).copy_from(people, mode: :hash)
~~~

## Streams from the file name

The extensions at the end of the file name name its streams, and IOStreams applies them in order: `example.csv.gz.pgp`
is decrypted with PGP, then decompressed with gzip. Only the registered extensions at the end of the name count, so
`data.gz.csv` and `report.csv.bak` have no streams. `#pipeline` lists them, from the one closest to your code to the
one closest to the stored data:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("somewhere/example.csv.gz.pgp")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:somewhere/example.csv.gz.pgp pipeline={gz: {}, pgp: {}}>

path.pipeline
# => {gz: {}, pgp: {}}
~~~

`#compressed?` and `#encrypted?` say whether a stream in the pipeline compresses or encrypts the data, whether it comes
from the file name or is set with `#stream`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz.pgp").compressed?
# => true

IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz.pgp").encrypted?
# => true
~~~

Compression within an encrypted file, such as PGP or Symmetric Encryption, is not reported, since only the encrypted
data records whether it was compressed.

### Option

`#option` sets the options of a stream, for when the file name includes it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

An option for a stream that the file name does not include has no effect, so the same code can supply the options of
every stream that a file might use, and read a PGP file, a Symmetric Encryption file, or a plain file, whichever the
configured path names:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("IMPORT_PATH")).option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

An option for a format applies to each of its extensions, so `option(:pgp, ...)` also applies to a `.gpg` file,
`option(:gz, ...)` to a `.gzip` file, and `option(:xlsx, ...)` to a `.xlsm` file. So a file name held in configuration
can change from one extension to the other without changing the code. When options are set for more than one
extension of a format, those for the extension in the file name take precedence.

`#setting` returns the options set for a stream:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase")
path.setting(:pgp)
# => {passphrase: "receiver_passphrase"}
~~~

### Options for reading and writing

The options of a stream are passed to its reader when reading, and to its writer when writing, and the two directions
usually take different options: the PGP writer needs the `recipient` to encrypt for, while the PGP reader needs the
`passphrase` of the private key. So that a path can be written and then read with the same options, each direction
ignores the options of the other that it does not need:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").
  option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org", passphrase: "receiver_passphrase")

path.write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
path.read
~~~

Reading ignores the options that only say how to write the file, such as the gzip compression `level`, or `compress`
for `.enc`, whose header records whether the file was compressed. Writing ignores the options that only say how to
read the file, such as the PGP `passphrase`.

Some options apply to both: `entry_file_name` names the file within a zip file when writing, and chooses the file to
read. The PGP `signer` signs the file when writing, and when reading requires that the file was signed by that key. An
option of one direction that the other could seem to use, but does not, such as the `sheet_name` of a spreadsheet,
which names the worksheet that is written, while reading always reads the first, raises `ArgumentError` in that
direction.

An option that neither direction accepts, such as a misspelled one, raises an `ArgumentError` that lists the valid
options as soon as it is set, even when the file name does not include that stream. So the same code reports it
wherever it runs, rather than only where the path, for example from configuration, includes that extension:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").option(:enc, compres: false)
# ArgumentError: Unknown option :compres for a :enc stream.
#   Valid options: :buffer_size, :version, :compress, :cipher_name, :header, :random_key, :random_iv.
~~~

### Stream

`#stream` replaces the streams that the file name implies, for example for a file whose name has none:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:zip).stream(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

The first stream set is the one closest to your code, so the file above is decrypted, and then unzipped:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:zip).stream(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").pipeline
# => {zip: {}, pgp: {passphrase: "receiver_passphrase"}}
~~~

`#stream` and `#option` cannot both be used on the same path. When the original file name is known, set it with
`#file_name` instead, so that IOStreams takes the streams and the format from it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").file_name("file.json.zip").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

## Streams of an IO

`IOStreams.stream(io)` reads or writes an IO that you supply, such as a `StringIO` or a socket, with the same methods
as a path. Set its file name, or its streams, since an IO has no name to take them from:

~~~ruby
io = StringIO.new
IOStreams.stream(io).file_name("example.csv.gz").writer(:hash) do |stream|
  stream << {name: "Jack", address: "There", zip_code: 1234}
  stream << {name: "Joe", zip_code: 1234, address: "Over There somewhere"}
end
~~~

IOStreams never closes an IO that you supply, so close it yourself when you are done with it.

A line, row or record writer that is already open, such as the one that `writer(:hash)` yields, can be handed to code
that calls `IOStreams.stream(io).writer(:hash)` itself, which then writes into it. Since the open writer writes with
its own settings, options, streams or an encoding supplied to that call raise `ArgumentError`.

---

# Tabular Formats

When reading or writing rows (`:array`) or records (`:hash`), IOStreams converts each line of the file to or from its
tabular format:

| Format | File name | Each row is |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| `:csv` | `.csv` | Comma separated values, quoted as needed. The default |
| `:psv` | `.psv` | Pipe separated values, without quoting |
| `:json` | `.json` | A JSON object on its own line, also called JSON Lines |
| `:fixed` | `.fixed`, or `format(:fixed)` | Fields at fixed positions in the line, see [Fixed width files](#fixed-width-files) |
| `:parquet` | `.parquet` | A row of an Apache Parquet file, which has no lines, see [Parquet files](#parquet-files) |

A spreadsheet, `.xlsx` or `.xlsm`, is read and written as CSV, one line for each row of its worksheet, see
[Excel spreadsheets](#excel-spreadsheets). Two more formats, `:array` and `:hash`, are for rows and records that are
already Ruby objects rather than text, such as those that another library passes, so they are not used for files.

## How the format is chosen {#format-inference}

The format of a file comes from the extensions of its name, after its first `.`, whatever their case, and the last one
that is a format wins, so `people.csv.gz` and `PEOPLE.CSV.PGP` are CSV, and `data.json.txt` is JSON:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sample.csv").each(:hash) { |record| p record }
IOStreams.path("sample.json.gz").each(:hash) { |record| p record }
~~~

The name of a directory, and the name of the file before its first `.`, are never its format, so `json/data.txt` and
`hash.txt` are not JSON or `:hash`. A file whose name has no format extension is CSV, the default, and a spreadsheet is
always CSV, whatever the rest of its name says.

### Setting the format {#specifying-the-format}

When the file name does not name the format, set it on the path with `#format`, which takes a Symbol, or the name of a
format as a String, such as one held in configuration:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sample_data").format(:json).each(:hash) { |record| p record }

IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("PEOPLE_PATH")).format(ENV.fetch("PEOPLE_FORMAT", "csv")).each(:hash) { |person| p person }
~~~

The format describes the file, so it is set on the path, rather than supplied to each call of `#each`, `#reader` or
`#writer`, which raises `ArgumentError` for `format:`. `#format` without an argument returns the format of the path.

## Records and rows without a schema

Without a [schema](#schema), every value is read as text, and written as its text:

* `each(:hash)` keys each record by the columns of the header row, cleansed: lower case, with spaces and dashes
  replaced with `_`, and other punctuation removed, while letters and digits of any language are kept. So the column
  `First Name` is the key `first_name`, `Zip-Code` is `zip_code`, `Amount ($)` is `amount_`, and `Prénom` is `prénom`.
  A column whose name has nothing left once cleansed, such as `#`, is skipped. JSON keys are used as they are.
* `each(:array)` yields the header row as it is, then each row of values. A JSON or Parquet file has no header row, so
  its first row is a header row of the keys of its first record, and each row after it the values of a record in
  that order, see [JSON files](#json-files).
* `writer(:hash)` takes the header row from the keys of the first record, so the values of a key that only a later
  record has are not written, except in JSON, where each record is written with its own keys.
* `writer(:array)` takes the first row written as the header row, which JSON writes no line for, since it only names
  the key of each value of the rows after it.
* A blank line is yielded as `nil`.

A schema names the columns, gives each its type, and says which columns a file can have and must have, so that the
keys no longer depend on how the cleansing changes a column, such as `Amount ($)` and `Amount (€)`, which both cleanse
to `amount_`.

## Schema

A schema gives the fields of the rows and records of a file, and the type of each one, so that reading them returns
each value as its type, such as an `Integer` or a `Date`, rather than as text, and writing them writes each value in
the text form of its type. It applies to every format, and gives the position of each field of a fixed width file.

A schema is a [Frictionless Table Schema](https://datapackage.org/standard/table-schema/), set on the path with
`#schema`, either as a Hash:

~~~ruby
# Read the id and joined columns of the file as their types, and skip its other columns.
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  fieldsMatch: "partial",
  fields:      [
    {name: "id",     type: "integer"},
    {name: "joined", type: "date"}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) { |person| p person }
# => {"id" => 42, "joined" => #<Date: 2026-10-13 ((2461327j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
~~~

Or as the path or url of a JSON file that holds it, in any store that IOStreams reads, so that the schema can be held
in configuration, like the path of the file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(ENV["PEOPLE_PATH"]).schema(ENV["PEOPLE_SCHEMA"]).each(:hash) { |person| p person }
~~~

The columns of the file are matched to the fields, and the keys of each record read are the names of its fields,
see [Matching columns to fields](#matching-columns-to-fields). `fieldsMatch: "partial"` above reads the fields that
the file has, and skips its other columns. Without `fieldsMatch`, as in Frictionless, the columns of the file must be
the fields, in order, which is what a file written with the schema has:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "id",     type: "integer"},
    {name: "pay",    type: "number", decimals: 2},
    {name: "joined", type: "date"},
    {name: "active", type: "boolean"}
  ]
)
path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"id" => 42, "pay" => BigDecimal("12.5"), "joined" => Date.new(2026, 10, 13), "active" => true}
end
path.read
# => "id,pay,joined,active\n42,12.50,2026-10-13,true\n"

path.each(:hash) { |person| p person }
# => {"id" => 42, "pay" => 0.125e2, "joined" => #<Date: 2026-10-13 ((2461327j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>, "active" => true}
~~~

A schema in a Hash is checked when it is set. A schema file is read the first time that a reader or writer needs it,
so that setting it does not read the file, and the copies of a path read it once. `#schema` returns the schema
that was set.

Like `#format`, the schema describes the file, so it is set on the path, rather than supplied to each call of
`#each`, `#reader` or `#writer`, which raises `ArgumentError` for `schema:`. Since it describes the columns of the
file, the deprecated options of each call that describe them without a schema, such as `columns:`, raise
`ArgumentError` with it, see [Upgrading](upgrading#the-column-options-of-each-call-are-deprecated).

### Types

| Type | Read as | Written as |
|------|---------|------------|
| `string` | a `String` | the text, or the text of any other value, except a `Hash` or an `Array`, which raise |
| `integer` | an `Integer`, from text such as `42`, `-12` or `0042`, or a whole number with a decimal point, such as `12.0`, as a spreadsheet stores it | `42` |
| `number` | a `BigDecimal`, from text such as `12.5`, `-1.5E3`, `NaN`, `INF` or `-INF`, or a number, including a `Rational`, or a `Float` with `floatNumber: true` | `12.5`, or `12.50` with `decimals: 2` |
| `boolean` | `true` or `false`, from one of its `trueValues` or `falseValues` | the first of its `trueValues` or `falseValues` |
| `date` | a `Date`, from `2026-10-13`, or text in its `format` | `2026-10-13`, or text in its `format` |
| `datetime` | a `Time`, from ISO 8601, such as `2026-10-13T09:30:00Z`, or text in its `format`. Text without an offset from UTC is read as UTC | ISO 8601, or text in its `format` |
| `any` | the value as it is read | the value, with a `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time` as its text, see [Values without a field](#values-without-a-field) |

A field without a `type` is `any`, as in Frictionless. Empty text is read as `nil`, except for a `string` or `any`
field, which keeps it.

A value that is not one of the type of its field, such as `N/A` for an `integer`, raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, naming the field and the value, both when reading and when writing. So does a `date`
or `datetime` that does not exist, such as `2026-02-30`.

JSON writes integers, numbers and booleans as JSON numbers and booleans, with all of the digits of a `number`, and the
digits after the decimal point that its `decimals` give, such as `12.50`, the same as CSV, and every other value as
text, such as a date, including in an application that uses ActiveSupport, as Rails does, which replaces how Ruby
writes JSON. Reading JSON keeps all of the digits of a `number` too, rather than reading it through a `Float`, while
the numbers of the other fields are a `Float`, as they are without a schema. The `:hash` and `:array` formats keep the
values themselves.

A `number` field needs the `bigdecimal` gem, which is a bundled gem from Ruby 3.4, so add `gem "bigdecimal"` to the
Gemfile, or set `floatNumber: true` to read a `Float` instead.

### Matching columns to fields

Each column of the header row, or key of a JSON record, is matched to the field:

1. Whose name is the column, such as `email` for the column `email`, whether the name is a String or a Symbol.
2. Whose `aliases` include the column, such as `["DOB", "Birth Date"]` for the field `date_of_birth`.
3. Whose name or alias is the same as the column once both are compared without their case, spaces and
   punctuation, and with the forms of a character that Unicode treats as the same made the same. So the field
   `first_name` matches the columns `First Name`, `FIRST.NAME` and `firstname`, the field `email` matches `E-mail`,
   and `id` matches the full width `ＩＤ` that some spreadsheets have.
4. Whose name or alias is the same as the column once both are cleansed as `cleanse_header` cleansed a header row, and
   then compared the same way. Cleansing drops the characters that Unicode otherwise makes digits, such as `²`, `½`
   and `①`, so that a field named as `cleanse_header` named its column, such as `area_m` for `Area (m²)`, matches
   it, as `area_m2` does.

The columns are matched once, when the header row is read, or once for each set of keys of the JSON records, which
are usually the same for every record, rather than for each value.

The keys of the records read are the names of their fields as they are given, so a field named with a Symbol, such as
`name: :id`, returns the key `:id`, whatever the column of the file is called. For a format with a header row, such
as CSV, `each(:array)` returns a header row of the names of the fields of its columns, and then the values of those
fields of each row, in the order of the fields. A file without a header row, such as JSON, Parquet or fixed width,
returns no header row: each row is the values of every field, in order, `nil` for a key that a JSON record does not
have. A column that the schema does not list is skipped, or raises, see [fieldsMatch](#fieldsmatch).

A column that could be either of two fields raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, rather than guess, such as
`amount` for the fields `Amount ($)` and `Amount (€)`, which match their own columns exactly. So do two columns that
are the same field, such as `email` and `Email`, rather than lose the value of one of them.

When writing, the header row is the names of the fields, in order, and the keys of each record written are matched
to the fields in the same way. `writer(:array)` takes the first row written as a header row, as `each(:array)`
returns one, and matches its columns to the fields in the same way, so that the values of each row after it can be in
any order, and the rows read from another file can be written as they are, such as by
`copy_from(source, mode: :array)`. A field that the header row does not have is written as empty. A file without a
header row, such as JSON, or a schema with `header: false`, takes rows of the values of the fields, in order, except
that `copy_from(source, mode: :array)` from a file with a header row, such as CSV, takes the columns of the rows from
its header row, rather than write it as a row of values.

So a file can have readable column names, while the code uses its own keys:

~~~ruby
report = IOStreams.path("report.csv").schema(fields: [{name: "First Name"}, {name: "Date of Birth", type: "date"}])
report.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {first_name: "Jack", date_of_birth: Date.new(2001, 2, 3)}
end
report.read
# => "First Name,Date of Birth\nJack,2001-02-03\n"
~~~

### fieldsMatch

`fieldsMatch` says how the columns of the file must match the fields, as Frictionless defines it:

| `fieldsMatch` | The columns of the file | Columns that the schema does not list |
|---------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| `exact`, the default | are the fields, in the same order | raise |
| `equal` | are the fields, in any order | raise |
| `subset` | include every field | are skipped |
| `superset` | are fields, but a field can be missing | raise |
| `partial` | include at least one field | are skipped |

A file that does not match raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, which lists each problem, such as the columns
that are not fields, and the fields that are missing. A column without a name, such as an empty column that a
spreadsheet exports after the last one, is a column that the schema does not list.

`partial` is the easiest to start with, and suits a schema that only gives the type of some of the columns. A schema
for files that are received from elsewhere, such as uploads, is usually stricter: `subset` accepts files with more
columns than the code needs, and `equal` or `exact` accept only the columns that the schema lists.

The keys of each JSON record are checked the same way, in any order. The columns of a file without a header row are
the fields in order, so `header: false` only accepts `exact`, and a fixed width file always has every field.

A row read that has a value after the last column of its header row, or after the last field of a file without one,
such as when a value has a comma that is not quoted, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` too, unless
`fieldsMatch` skips it, rather than lose the value. A blank value there, such as after a comma at the end of each
line, is not data, so it is ignored.

A file that is written always has every field, so writing only checks the keys of each record, the columns of the
header row of the rows written, and the values of each row after the last field or column: `subset` and `partial`
skip them, and the others raise `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`. A field that a record does not supply is written
as empty, or as `null` in JSON.

### Required fields

A field whose `constraints` are `required`, as Frictionless defines it, must have a value: a header row, or JSON
record, without the field raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, whatever `fieldsMatch` is, and a value that is
`nil`, or empty text, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, both when reading and when writing, including a blank
record or row written, such as `{}`, which is otherwise written as a blank line. Text that is only spaces is a value
for a `string` field, as in Frictionless, but not for a type that reads it as `nil`, such as an `integer`.

~~~ruby
# An upload, whose columns may be in any order, with names that people typed, and columns that the code ignores.
schema = {
  fieldsMatch: "subset",
  fields:      [
    {name: "first_name",    constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "email",         aliases: ["E-mail Address"], constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "date_of_birth", type: "date", aliases: ["DOB", "Birth Date"]}
  ]
}
IOStreams.path("upload.csv").schema(schema).each(:hash) { |contact| p contact }
# "E-mail Address,FIRST NAME,DOB,Notes" =>
# {"first_name" => "Jack", "email" => "j@x.com", "date_of_birth" => #<Date: 2001-02-03 ((2451944j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
~~~

IOStreams does not support the other constraints of Frictionless yet, such as `maxLength`, so they raise
`ArgumentError`, rather than appear to check values that they do not.

### Schema properties

* `fields` The fields of the file, in the order of its columns. Required.
* `fieldsMatch` How the columns of the file must match the fields, see [fieldsMatch](#fieldsmatch). Default: `exact`
* `header` `false` when the file has no header row, as in a Frictionless Table Dialect. The columns of the file are
  then the fields, in order: reading takes every line as a row, and writing writes no header row, and the fields in
  order. A format without a header row, such as JSON or fixed width, ignores it. Default: `true`
* `width` The length of every line of a fixed width file, see [Fixed width files](#fixed-width-files).

`$schema`, `title` and `description` describe the schema to people and have no effect.

~~~ruby
# A CSV file without a header row.
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(header: false, fields: [{name: "name"}, {name: "age", type: "integer"}])
path.each(:hash) { |person| p person }
# => {"name" => "Jack", "age" => 21}
~~~

Since the schema is set on the path, every reader of the path reads the file the same way, including `#copy_from`
and `#copy_to`, whose options only apply to the target.

### Field properties

* `name` The key of the field in each record, and its column in the header row written. Required.
* `type` See [Types](#types). Default: `any`
* `constraints` `{required: true}` for a field that must have a value, see [Required fields](#required-fields).
* `format` For a `date` or a `datetime`, the strptime pattern of its text, such as `"%d/%m/%Y"` or `"%Y%m%d"`.
  Default: ISO 8601.
* `trueValues` and `falseValues` For a `boolean`, the text that is true and false.
  Default: `["true", "True", "TRUE", "1"]` and `["false", "False", "FALSE", "0"]`
* `floatNumber` For a `number`, `true` to read a `Float` rather than a `BigDecimal`, as frictionless-py does.
* `aliases` The other names of the column of the field, see [Matching columns to fields](#matching-columns-to-fields).
  IOStreams adds this property.
* `decimals` For a `number`, the number of digits to write after the decimal point, rounding a `BigDecimal` half up,
  and a `Float`, with `floatNumber: true`, as Ruby's `format` does, to the nearest of its binary value, as the layouts
  of fixed width files always have. IOStreams adds this property.
* `width`, `start` and `truncate` The position of the field in a fixed width file, see
  [Fixed width files](#fixed-width-files). IOStreams adds these properties. The other formats ignore them, so that
  one schema can describe both a fixed width file and the CSV file that it is converted to.

`title`, `description`, `example` and `rdfType` describe a field to people and have no effect, as do the properties
of other tools, whose names include a `:`, such as `"mytool:owner"`. Any other property raises `ArgumentError`, as do
the parts of Frictionless that IOStreams does not support yet, such as `missingValues`, `primaryKey`, the constraints
other than `required`, and the `time` type, so that a schema never appears to check a value that it does not.

### Values without a field

A value of a file without a schema, or of a field without a type, is written as a field of type `any` writes it:

| Value | Written as |
|-------|------------|
| `BigDecimal` | a plain decimal, such as `12.5`, rather than `0.125e2` |
| `Time` or `DateTime` | ISO 8601, such as `2026-10-13T09:30:00Z`, with as many digits of its fraction of a second as it needs |
| `Date` | ISO 8601, such as `2026-10-13` |
| any other value | its `to_s`, such as `42` or `true` |

JSON writes a `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time` as that text, within an object or an array too, so that a `BigDecimal`
keeps all of its digits, and writes every other value as itself, such as a number or `true`. The `:hash` and `:array`
formats keep the values themselves. To write a value in another form, such as a date as `13/10/2026`, give its field
a type and a `format` in the schema.

## CSV and PSV files

CSV values are quoted when they hold a comma, a quote or a line break, so a quoted value can hold a line break, which
stays within its row, see [Lines](streams#lines). `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)` read CSV a line at a time, and
parse each line directly, which is several times faster than `CSV.parse_line`, while giving the same values.

PSV separates values with `|`, and has no quoting, so it is simpler and a little faster to parse. Since a value cannot
hold a `|` or a line break, writing PSV replaces a `|` within a value with `:`, and a line break with a space, so that a
value cannot add columns or records:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.psv").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack", "note" => "a|b\nc"}
end

IOStreams.path("example.psv").read
# => "name|note\nJack|a:b c\n"
~~~

In CSV, a value that is empty is read as `nil`, and a quoted empty value, `""`, as an empty String.

## JSON files

A JSON file holds one JSON object on each line, the format called JSON Lines, so that it can be read a record at a
time. A file that holds one JSON array of every record is not supported, since it would have to be read whole.

Each record is read with its own keys, as they are in the file, and its values keep their JSON types: a number is an
Integer or a Float, and `true`, `false` and `null` are `true`, `false` and `nil`. A line that is not an object, such
as `[1, 2]`, raises `IOStreams::Errors::TypeMismatch`, and a line of `null` or `{}` is read as `nil`, like a blank
line. Writing writes each record as a JSON object, with a `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time` as its usual text, see
[Values without a field](#values-without-a-field).

A JSON file has no header row, so the first row that `each(:array)` yields is a header row of the keys of its first
record, and each row after it holds the values of a record in that order, `nil` for a key that it does not have:

~~~ruby
# people.json holds:
# {"name":"Jack","age":21}
# {"name":"Jill"}
IOStreams.path("people.json").each(:array) { |row| p row }
# ["name", "age"]
# ["Jack", 21]
# ["Jill", nil]
~~~

A record with a key that the first record does not have raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, since no row has a
column for it, so read records whose keys vary with `each(:hash)`, or describe them with a schema whose
`fieldsMatch` is `"superset"`. With a schema, each row is the values of its fields, in order, without a header row.
`writer(:array)` takes the first row written as the header row, which names the key of each value of the rows after
it, without a line of its own, so that the rows read can be written again, or copied into another format, see
[Copying and moving](copy_files):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.json").writer(:array) do |io|
  io << ["name", "age"]
  io << ["Jack", 21]
end

IOStreams.path("people.json").read
# => "{\"name\":\"Jack\",\"age\":21}\n"
~~~

## Excel spreadsheets

A spreadsheet is read as CSV, one line for each row of its first worksheet, so the `:line`, `:array` and `:hash` modes
apply, and a schema can give the type of each column:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("spreadsheet.xlsx").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

Each cell is read as its text: a date as `2026-01-02`, a time as its time of day in UTC, such as
`2026-01-02T09:30:00Z`, since Excel holds a time without a time zone, and a number as Excel stores it, as a decimal,
such as `1.0` or `12.5`, which an `integer` field reads as `1`. A date in a custom number format, such as one written
with `auto_format: true`, reads as a time, such as `2026-01-02T00:00:00Z`, which a `date` field does not read: only
Excel's built-in date formats read as a date. Reading needs the `creek` gem.

Writing writes the CSV text of each row into the cells of a workbook with one worksheet, with the `xlsxtream` gem:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("report.xlsx").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack", "zip" => "01234"}
  io << {"name" => "Jill", "zip" => "98101"}
end
~~~

Every cell is written as text by default, so that reading the spreadsheet returns the same values, such as the leading
zero of `"01234"`, with these exceptions:

* Empty cells at the end of a row are not stored, so they read back as missing values, which are nil, as for CSV.
* A row of only empty cells reads back as an empty line, which `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)` yield as nil.
* A carriage return within a value reads back as a newline, since XML reads a line break within text as a newline.

The writer accepts these options:

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `sheet_name` | `"Sheet1"` | The name of the worksheet: 1 to 31 characters, without any of `[ ] : * ? / \`, and not starting or ending with an apostrophe, as Excel requires. Any other name raises `ArgumentError` before the file is opened. |
| `auto_format` | `false` | Write values that look like numbers, dates, times or booleans, such as `"1.5"`, `"2026-10-09"` or `"true"`, as Excel numbers, dates and booleans. Such values may then read back differently, such as `"01234"` as `"1234.0"`. |
| `use_shared_strings` | `false` | Store each distinct value once, which makes the workbook smaller when values repeat, but holds every distinct value in memory until the workbook is complete. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("report.xlsx").option(:xlsx, sheet_name: "Totals", auto_format: true).writer(:array) do |io|
  io << ["region", "total"]
  io << ["West", 1250.75]
end
~~~

Notes:

* Reading ignores `auto_format` and `use_shared_strings`, since the workbook records them, and raises for `sheet_name`,
  since it always reads the first worksheet.
* Reading a spreadsheet needs a local file, so one stored elsewhere, or within another stream, is copied into a temp
  file first, and its rows are converted into CSV in a second temp file, since the `creek` gem returns them to a
  block. Writing streams the workbook, without a temp file, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used).
* On JRuby, `creek` reads a value that holds a line break only up to the line break, unless the workbook was written
  with `use_shared_strings: true`, as Excel does.

## Parquet files

[Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) files hold the type of each column, so their records are read with typed
values, such as an `Integer`, `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time`, even without a schema. A `.parquet` file name selects the
format, and it can also be compressed or encrypted, such as `data.parquet.pgp`. Install the
[parquet](https://github.com/njaremko/parquet-ruby) gem, which is not available on JRuby.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://bucket/people.parquet").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
  # => {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack", "amount" => 0.1235e2, "born" => #<Date: 2000-02-29 ((2451604j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
end
~~~

With a schema, the columns are matched to its fields, and each value is converted to the type of its field, as for any
other format, see [Schema](#schema).

Writing needs a schema, since a Parquet file records the type of each of its columns. Its fields are the columns, and
each type is written as:

| Type | Parquet type |
|------|--------------|
| `string` | `string` |
| `integer` | `int64` |
| `number` | `decimal(38, decimals)`, rounding each value to its `decimals`, or `double` with `floatNumber: true` |
| `boolean` | `boolean` |
| `date` | `date32` |
| `datetime` | `timestamp_micros`, adjusted to UTC, so it is read back in UTC |

A `number` field needs `decimals` or `floatNumber: true`, since a Parquet decimal has a fixed number of digits after
its point, and a field of type `any` raises `ArgumentError`, since it has no type. A field whose `constraints` are
`required` is written as a column that cannot be null.

~~~ruby
schema = {
  fields: [
    {name: "id", type: "integer", constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "name", type: "string"},
    {name: "amount", type: "number", decimals: 2},
    {name: "born", type: "date"}
  ]
}

IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).writer(:hash) do |writer|
  writer << {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack", "amount" => BigDecimal("12.35"), "born" => Date.new(2000, 2, 29)}
end

# Convert a CSV file into Parquet
IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).copy_from(IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(schema), mode: :hash)
~~~

Set how its columns are compressed with `option(:parquet, compression: ...)`: `"none"`, `"snappy"`, the default,
`"gzip"`, `"lz4"`, `"zstd"` or `"brotli"`. Reading finds the compression in the file, so it ignores the option, and so
does a file that is not Parquet, as for the options of other streams. `stream(:parquet, ...)` sets it too, and still
applies the streams in the file name, such as `.gz` in `people.parquet.gz`, since Parquet is not one of them.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).option(:parquet, compression: "zstd").writer(:hash) do |writer|
  writer << {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack"}
end
~~~

A Parquet file stores each column on its own, so with a schema whose `fieldsMatch` is `"subset"` or `"partial"`, which
skip the columns that it does not list, only the columns of its fields are read and decoded, which is faster for a
wide file. The other values of `fieldsMatch` read every column, so that they can check the others.

A Parquet file records its columns at its end, so it is read from a local file, and a file stored elsewhere, such as
on S3, is first copied into a temp file. Likewise it is written to a temp file, which is then copied to the path. The
records written before the block leaves early, such as with `break`, are kept, as for other formats, and nothing is
written when the block raises, or when the thread writing it is killed. Writing without a schema, with a field that
has no Parquet type, or with a compression that Parquet does not have, raises `ArgumentError` before the file is
opened, so that an existing file is kept.

A value that its column cannot hold raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, naming its field, when the record is
written: an integer outside the range of an `int64`, or a number with more digits before its decimal point than its
`decimal(38, decimals)` holds, that is `38 - decimals`.

A Parquet file has no lines, so the `:line` mode, and the `delimiter:` and `embedded_within:` options, raise
`ArgumentError`, and so does `#encoding`, since its values are not text, which the `parquet` gem reads and writes as
UTF-8. Like JSON, it has no header row, so without a schema the first row that `each(:array)` yields is a header row
of its columns, and with a schema each row is the values of its fields, in order, without a header row:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://bucket/people.parquet").each(:array) { |row| p row }
# ["id", "name", "amount", "born"]
# [1, "Jack", 0.1235e2, #<Date: 2000-02-29 ((2451604j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>]
~~~

## Fixed width files

Fixed width files have no delimiters; each field is at the same position in every line. Since the positions cannot be
inferred from the file, the schema gives the `width` of each field, in the order of the line:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("sample_data").format(:fixed).schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name",    type: "string",  width: 23},
    {name: "address", type: "string",  width: 40},
    {name: "zip",     type: "integer", width: 5}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) { |record| p record }
~~~

Writing a fixed width file uses the same schema to render each record:

~~~ruby
path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "address" => "Somewhere", "zip" => 12345}
end
~~~

A fixed width file has no header row, so each row that `each(:array)` yields is the values of the fields, in order,
and `writer(:array)` takes rows the same way:

~~~ruby
path.each(:array) { |row| p row }
# ["Jack Jones", "Somewhere", 12345]
~~~

The schema can be held in a file, such as this `people.schema.json`:

~~~json
{
  "fields": [
    {"name": "name",    "type": "string",  "width": 23, "truncate": true},
    {"name": "address", "type": "string",  "width": 40},
    {"name": "zip",     "type": "integer", "width": 5,  "start": 66},
    {"name": "weight",  "type": "number",  "width": 10, "decimals": 2},
    {"name": "joined",  "type": "date",    "width": 8,  "format": "%Y%m%d"},
    {"name": "notes",   "type": "string",  "width": "remainder"}
  ]
}
~~~

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.txt").format(:fixed).schema("people.schema.json").each(:hash) { |person| p person }
~~~

The properties that place each field:

* `width` The number of characters of the field. The last field may have a width of `"remainder"` to take the rest
  of the line.
* `start` The position of the first character of the field, counting from 1, as the specifications of fixed width
  files do. It skips the characters after the field before it, such as a filler: in the example above, `zip` starts
  at 66, which skips the 2 characters after the 63 characters of `name` and `address`.
  Default: right after the field before it.
* `truncate` For a `string`, `true` to write only the first `width` characters of a longer value. Without it, a value
  that is too long raises `IOStreams::Errors::ValueTooLong`. A number is never truncated, and raises instead.

The `width` at the top level of the schema is the length of every line, when the line ends after the last field, such
as after a filler, for example `{"fields": [...], "width": 94}`. A `width` of `"remainder"` accepts lines of any
length, ignoring what follows the last field. Otherwise every line ends where the last field ends. A line of another
length raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLineLength`.

When reading, each value is the text of its field without its leading and trailing spaces, converted to the type of
its field. The keys of each record are the names of the fields as they are given, so that a field whose name is a
Symbol returns a Symbol key.

When writing, a number is right justified and zero filled, and a missing number is written as zero, as the
specifications of most fixed width files require. A number that is not finite, such as `NaN` or `-INF`, is space
filled instead, so that it can be read back. Any other value is left justified and space filled, with each line
break replaced with a space, so that a value cannot add records. The characters that no field covers, such as a
filler, are spaces. The keys of the records written may be strings or symbols.

### Character encoding

Fixed width files are read and written as ASCII by default. The programs that write them, such as
COBOL programs, and the formats that specify them, such as NACHA ACH and IRS FIRE, count each column's
size in bytes, and their text is ASCII, or a single-byte code page such as ISO-8859-1. So a value read
is a UTF-8 string, like the values of every other format, and any byte that is not ASCII raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, naming the byte and its offset, rather than shifting every
column that follows it.

Each `width` counts the characters of the text as it is read, and when writing, string values are
padded and truncated to `width` characters. In ASCII, and in a single-byte code page, each character
is one byte, so the widths count bytes.

Set the encoding of the file with [`#encoding`](streams#character-encoding) when it is not
ASCII. An encoding that is set always replaces the ASCII default, and `#raw` reads and writes the bytes as
they are stored:

* A single-byte code page, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252, or EBCDIC from a mainframe: name it
  with the encoding that the values are read as, for example
  `encoding("ISO-8859-1:UTF-8")`, `"Windows-1252:UTF-8"`, or `"IBM037:UTF-8"` for
  EBCDIC. The widths count bytes, and the values are UTF-8 strings.
* To load a file anyway, replacing each byte that is not ASCII with a space, so that the columns stay
  aligned: `encoding(replace: " ")`.
* UTF-8 written by a program that counts characters: `encoding("UTF-8")`.
* UTF-8 written by a program that counts bytes, which is rare: read it as binary, with
  `encoding("BINARY")`, whose values are binary strings, or with `replace: " "`.

An EBCDIC file is split into lines after it is converted, so its lines must end with the EBCDIC line
feed (`0x25`), which converts to `\n`. The EBCDIC new line (`0x15`) converts to U+0085, so supply
`delimiter: "\u0085"` to `#each` or `#reader` for a file whose lines end with it.

The `:line` mode reads ASCII too when the format of the path is `:fixed`, set with `#format` or
detected from a file name such as `data.fixed`.

When writing, a value that is not ASCII raises `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`, rather than
writing a line that is longer than the schema in bytes. Set the encoding of the file, such as
`encoding("ISO-8859-1")`, whose lines are then the length of the schema in bytes, or
`replace: " "` to write a space for each character that is not ASCII:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.txt").encoding("ISO-8859-1")
path.format(:fixed).schema(fields: [{name: "name", width: 10}, {name: "zip", width: 5}])
path.writer(:hash) { |io| io << {"name" => "José", "zip" => "12345"} }
~~~

### Cleaning fixed width files

To remove non-printable characters, such as NUL padding, from a fixed width file, replace them with a
space, so that every column after them stays in place:

~~~ruby
path.encoding(cleaner: :replace_non_printable, replace: " ")
~~~

Since `replace:` also replaces invalid characters, each byte that is not ASCII is replaced with a space
too, unless the encoding of the file is set.

The `:printable` cleaner removes non-printable characters rather than replacing them, even with
`replace:`, which only replaces invalid characters. So each one it removes moves every column that
follows it, and a line with one raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLineLength`.

---

# Compression and Encryption

The extensions at the end of a file name say how the file is compressed or encrypted, and IOStreams reads and writes
the file through the stream of each one, a block at a time. `example.csv.gz.pgp` is compressed with gzip and then
encrypted with PGP, so reading it decrypts it, and then decompresses it. How a file name becomes a pipeline of streams,
and how to set the streams of a file whose name has none, is explained in
[Streams from the file name](streams#streams-from-the-file-name).

| Extension | Stream | Needs | Options when reading | Options when writing |
|-----------|--------|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `.gz`, `.gzip` | [gzip](#gzip) | Nothing: `zlib` is part of Ruby | None | `level` |
| `.bz2` | [bzip2](#bzip2) | The `bzip2-ffi` gem | `small`, `first_only`, `autoclose` | `block_size`, `work_factor`, `autoclose` |
| `.zip` | [Zip](#zip) | The `rubyzip` gem to read, and `zip_kit` to write | `entry_file_name` | `entry_file_name` |
| `.zst` | [Zstandard](#zstandard) | The `zstd-ruby` gem, 2.0.0 or later, or on JRuby the zstd-jni jar | None | `level` |
| `.enc` | [Symmetric Encryption](#symmetric-encryption) | The `symmetric-encryption` gem, with its ciphers configured | `version`, `buffer_size` | `compress`, `version`, `cipher_name`, `header`, `random_key`, `random_iv` |
| `.pgp`, `.gpg` | [PGP](#pgp) | The `gpg` program of GnuPG | `passphrase`, `signer` and more, see [Reader options](pgp#reader-options) | `recipient`, `signer` and more, see [Writer options](pgp#writer-options) |
| `.xlsx`, `.xlsm` | [Excel spreadsheets](#excel-spreadsheets) | The `creek` gem to read, and `xlsxtream` to write | None | `sheet_name`, `auto_format`, `use_shared_strings` |

Only the registered extensions at the end of the name count, after its first `.`, whatever their case, so
`DATA.CSV.GZ` is compressed with gzip, while `data.gz.csv` and `report.csv.bak` have no streams. `IOStreams.extensions`
returns the format registered for each extension:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.extensions.keys
# => [:bz2, :enc, :gz, :gzip, :zip, :pgp, :gpg, :xlsx, :xlsm, :zst]
~~~

IOStreams does not depend on any of these gems, so add to the Gemfile those of the streams that your application uses.
Each one is loaded when its stream is first used, and a gem that is not installed raises `LoadError`, naming it:

~~~
LoadError: Please install the gem 'bzip2-ffi' to support Bzip2. cannot load such file -- bzip2/ffi
~~~

## Setting options

Set the options of a stream on the path with `#option`, and they apply when the file name includes that stream:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 9).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
~~~

* An option for a stream that the file name does not include has no effect, so the same code can set the options of
  every stream that a path held in configuration might use.
* An option for a format applies to each of its extensions: `option(:gz, ...)` to a `.gzip` file, `option(:pgp, ...)`
  to a `.gpg` file, and `option(:xlsx, ...)` to a `.xlsm` file.
* For a file whose name does not name its streams, set them with `#stream`, which takes the same options, such as
  `IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:gz, level: 9)`, see [Stream](streams#stream).

The name of each option is checked when it is set. An option that neither the reader nor the writer of the stream
takes raises `ArgumentError`, which lists the valid options, even when the file name does not include that stream, so
a misspelled option is reported wherever the code runs:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").option(:gz, levle: 9)
# ArgumentError: Unknown option :levle for a :gz stream. Valid options: :level.
~~~

The value of each option is checked when the file is written, before it is opened. So a value that a stream cannot
write with, such as a gzip `level` that is out of range, or a stream whose gem is not installed, raises before an
existing file is replaced:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 10).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
# ArgumentError: Invalid gzip level 10: supply an Integer from 0, no compression, to 9, the best compression, or -1 for the default
~~~

What only the stream itself can find out, such as whether gpg has the key of a PGP recipient, raises once the file has
been opened, and the write fails like any other, see [Writing](streams#writing).

### Options for reading and writing

One set of options is shared by the reader and the writer of a stream, so that a path can be written and then read.
Each direction ignores the options of the other, such as the gzip `level` when reading, or the PGP `passphrase` when
writing, and the table above lists the options that each direction uses:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.csv.bz2").option(:bz2, block_size: 1, small: true)
path.write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
path.read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

An option of the writer that a reader could seem to use, but does not, raises when reading, rather than being ignored:
the `sheet_name` of a spreadsheet, since reading always reads the first worksheet. See
[Options for reading and writing](streams#options-for-reading-and-writing).

## Compression {#compression-options}

Each compression stream compresses the data as it is written, and decompresses it as it is read, so that a file of any
size is processed a block at a time. Zip is the exception when reading: a zip file lists its contents at its end, so
reading one needs the whole file on local disk.

### gzip

gzip uses `zlib`, which is part of Ruby.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `level` | Writing | -1, zlib's default, which is 6 | The compression level, from 0, no compression, to 9, the best compression. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 9).writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

Reading returns the data of every member of a gzip file, as `gunzip` does, so gzip files that were joined, such as with
`cat a.gz b.gz > ab.gz`, are read as one file. Zero bytes after the last member, which some programs add, are ignored,
while any other data after it raises `Zlib::GzipFile::Error`, with the message `not in gzip format`.

### bzip2

bzip2 uses the `bzip2-ffi` gem, which calls the bzip2 library, libbz2, of the system.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `block_size` | Writing | 9 | The size of the blocks that are compressed, from 1, 100KB, to 9, 900KB. A larger block compresses better, and uses more memory. |
| `work_factor` | Writing | 0, libbz2's default, which is 30 | How hard to try with data that repeats a lot before using a slower algorithm, from 0 to 250. |
| `small` | Reading | `false` | Decompress with an algorithm that uses less memory, about 2,300KB less, at about half the speed. |
| `first_only` | Reading | `false` | Read only the first bzip2 stream of a file that holds several, such as bzip2 files that were joined. By default every one is read. |
| `autoclose` | Both | `false` | Close the IO beneath the bzip2 stream when the stream ends, such as an IO supplied to `IOStreams.stream`, which IOStreams otherwise leaves open, see [When writing fails](#when-writing-fails). |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.bz2").option(:bz2, block_size: 1).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
~~~

### Zip

Reading a `.zip` file reads one file within it: the first file, skipping any folders, or the file that
`entry_file_name` names, including its folders:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("offices.zip").option(:zip, entry_file_name: "data/offices.csv").each(:hash) do |office|
  p office
end
~~~

Reading uses the `rubyzip` gem. JRuby reads zip files with Java's own support instead, so it does not need `rubyzip`.

A zip file lists its contents at its end, so it is read from a local file. A local path, and the temp file that an
SFTP path downloads into, are read where they are, while a zip file on S3 or HTTP, or within another stream, such as
`example.csv.zip.pgp`, is first copied into a temp file, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used).

Reading raises `IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure`, naming the zip file by the name of the file that is read, such as
its path, the key of an S3 object or the path of a url, tagged with the kind of failure, which is the same on every
platform, see [Errors](errors#what-each-stream-raises):

* `IOStreams::Errors::MissingEntry` when the zip file does not contain the file to read: one of only folders, or one
  without the file that `entry_file_name` names, or where it names a folder:

  ~~~
  IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure: The zip file /data/offices.zip does not contain the file "data/missing.csv"
  ~~~

* `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt` when the file within it is corrupt: once all of it has been read, its size, or its
  CRC32 checksum, is not the one that the zip file records. So the block has already read the corrupt data, as with
  any check that needs the whole file:

  ~~~
  IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure: The file "data.csv" within the zip file /data/a.zip is corrupt: invalid entry CRC (expected 0x9d0b854a but got 0x1e367632)
  ~~~

A file that is not a zip file, or data that cannot be decompressed, also raises an exception tagged as
`IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, naming the zip file too.

Writing uses the `zip_kit` gem, which streams the zip file as it is written, without a temp file, even to S3, or into
another stream, such as `example.csv.zip.pgp`. The zip file holds one file, which is named after the path, without the
`.zip` extension and any that follow it, so `example.csv.zip` and `example.csv.zip.pgp` both hold `example.csv`.
`entry_file_name` names it instead, and a stream without a file name, such as one supplied to `IOStreams.stream`, names
it `file`.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `entry_file_name` | Both | Reading: the first file. Writing: the name of the path without `.zip`, or `file` | The name of the file within the zip file, including its folders, such as `data/offices.csv`. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("export.zip").option(:zip, entry_file_name: "people.csv").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

`zip_file_name`, which earlier versions took when writing, raises `ArgumentError`: use `entry_file_name`.

### Zstandard

Zstandard uses the `zstd-ruby` gem, 2.0.0 or later, which decompresses one zstd block, 128KB, at a time, however well
the data compresses. IOStreams uses its `Zstd::StreamingCompress` and `Zstd::StreamingDecompress`, rather than its
`Zstd::StreamWriter` and `Zstd::StreamReader`, which the
[zstd-ruby README marks as experimental](https://github.com/SpringMT/zstd-ruby#stream-writer-and-reader-wrapper).

JRuby cannot load `zstd-ruby`, which is a C extension, so on JRuby IOStreams uses the
[zstd-jni](https://github.com/luben/zstd-jni) jar instead, which the application adds to the classpath, for example
with jar-dependencies, which is part of JRuby:

~~~ruby
require_jar "com.github.luben", "zstd-jni", "1.5.7-3"
~~~

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `level` | Writing | 3, zstd's default | The compression level, from 1, the fastest, to 22, the best compression, or a negative level, down to -131072, for faster compression still. 0 selects the default. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.zst").option(:zst, level: 19).writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

* Reading returns the data of every frame of a zstd file, as `zstd -d` does, so zstd files that were joined are read
  as one file.
* Reading checks the checksum of each frame that has one, such as a frame that the `zstd` command wrote, and raises
  `RuntimeError` when the data does not match it. On JRuby each frame that IOStreams writes has a checksum, as the
  `zstd` command writes it. On MRI it does not, since `zstd-ruby` cannot write one.
* Empty data is not zstd, so reading it raises `RuntimeError: zstd decompress error: the data is empty`, as
  `zstd -d` does.
* On MRI, a file that was cut short, such as by an interrupted download, is not detected: reading returns the data up
  to where the file ends. zstd-jni on JRuby detects it, and raises `RuntimeError`.

## Encryption

### Symmetric Encryption

`.enc` encrypts with the [Symmetric Encryption](https://encryption.reidmorrison.com/) gem, `symmetric-encryption`,
using the ciphers that the application configures for it, such as in `config/symmetric-encryption.yml` in a Rails
application. When no cipher is configured, reading raises `SymmetricEncryption::ConfigError`, and so does writing,
before the file is opened.

By default each file is compressed with gzip, and then encrypted with a random key and IV of its own. The header at
the start of the file holds them, the key encrypted with the configured cipher, and records whether the data is
compressed, so reading needs no options:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.enc").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "ssn" => "123-45-6789"}
end

IOStreams.path("example.csv.enc").each(:hash) { |record| p record }
# => {"name" => "Jack Jones", "ssn" => "123-45-6789"}
~~~

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `compress` | Writing | `true` | Compress the data with gzip before encrypting it. Set `false` for data that is already compressed. |
| `version` | Both | The primary cipher | When writing, the version of the configured cipher to encrypt with. When reading a file without a header, the version of the cipher to decrypt it with, since the header otherwise names it. |
| `cipher_name` | Writing | The cipher of `version` | The OpenSSL cipher to encrypt the data with, such as `"aes-256-cbc"`, with a random key and IV. |
| `random_key` | Writing | `true` | Encrypt with a random key, which the header holds encrypted. Needs `random_iv: true`. |
| `random_iv` | Writing | `true` | Encrypt with a random IV, which the header holds. |
| `header` | Writing | `true` | Write the header. A file is only written without one with `compress: false`, `random_key: false` and `random_iv: false`. |
| `buffer_size` | Reading | 16384 | The number of bytes to read from the file at a time. |

A `version` that is not configured raises `SymmetricEncryption::CipherError` before the file is opened.

### PGP

`.pgp` and `.gpg` files are encrypted, decrypted, signed and verified with the `gpg` program of GnuPG, which must be
installed wherever they are read or written. Writing needs the recipient to encrypt the file for, and reading the
passphrase of the recipient's private key:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org").write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")

IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

See [PGP Encryption](pgp) for creating and importing keys, signing and verifying files, and every option.

## Excel spreadsheets

A spreadsheet, `.xlsx` or `.xlsm`, is read as CSV, one line for each row of its first worksheet, and written from CSV
into a workbook with one worksheet. So the `:line`, `:array` and `:hash` modes apply, and the format of its rows is
always CSV. See [Excel spreadsheets](formats#excel-spreadsheets) for the values that each cell is read as.

### Reading an Excel spreadsheet

Reading uses the `creek` gem, which reads a local file and returns its rows to a block, so the rows are converted into
CSV in a temp file for your code to read. A spreadsheet on S3 or HTTP, or within another stream, is first copied into a
temp file of its own, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used). Reading takes no options, and
raises `ArgumentError` for `sheet_name`, since it always reads the first worksheet.

### Writing an Excel spreadsheet
